s: Routes users to the best region using health, geography, and latency - the switchboard of a multi-region deployment.
w: It answers DNS or anycast-edge queries with region endpoints. Health checks continuously probe each region; when one fails its weight shifts to survivors within seconds-to-minutes. Steering policies include geo-proximity, latency-based, weighted-canary, and failover priority. Sessions that need regional affinity rely on consistent user-to-region mapping.
use: Active-active multi-region serving where users hit the nearest healthy region
Disaster recovery: automatic traffic drain from a failed region
Canarying a new region with 1% of traffic before full cutover
Compliance routing - EU users land in EU regions only
avoid: Per-request routing decisions - it steers at connection/DNS granularity, not per API call
Stateful flows that assume all requests from one session hit one region unless you also replicate session state

size.rps_per_instance: Managed service scales transparently; cost is per query

pat.d: All regions serve read-write traffic; GLB absorbs failures invisibly to users.

pits: DNS caching delays failover - set TTLs low (30-60s) during migration windows, accept resolver stickiness otherwise
Health-check false positives flap traffic - require multiple consecutive failures
Regional DB failover lags traffic failover - sequence carefully to avoid writes hitting a region with stale data
tips: Always pair with a story about data layer: traffic failover is easy, consistent data failover is the real problem
Know RTO/RPO vocabulary when discussing region evacuation
